Preface

Scrolling back through my publishing history, I realized I haven’t written a proper article in nearly three years. The last “serious” one was my review of 2021: Ziyu Acoustics: 2021 in review. That post also marked the end of my fortnightly publishing streak. Since then I have only reposted the odd video or English-language article, just to remind people the account still exists.

Reading a few recent issues of audioXpress has made me want to write again. I have spent the last three years with my head down in a new job. Audio is a branch of acoustics, but once I got deep into it I found it very different from the acoustics I had worked on before, and I was back to being a beginner, much as when I first started studying acoustics. Now that I have built up a little experience and lift my head, I realize how little I know about where the industry as a whole is going. In the years when I wrote regularly for the account, I first used up everything I already knew; after that, keeping to the schedule meant constantly reading new material, or I would have had nothing to write about, and that pushed me to keep up with the field. So I want to start writing again partly to satisfy the urge to put something out, and partly to use the process to keep pace with the industry and not fall behind.

The plan for now: take audioXpress articles that interest me as a starting point, translate parts of them, and write the rest from what I already know and what I learn along the way. Let’s see how far it goes!

In the era of the software-defined vehicle, audio is becoming a new arena for innovation and differentiation. OEMs now need advanced audio software platforms to develop, deploy and upgrade audio features over the entire life of the vehicle, and to work out what this means for new business models and opportunities.

— Jose Maria Marin, BlackBerry QNX

The 5th AES International Conference on Automotive Audio took place in Gothenburg in June 2024. I had applied to attend, but in the end I couldn’t go, for various reasons. From three demo cars and 50 attendees at the first edition in 2009, the conference has grown to more than 20 cars and 330 attendees this year.

Even that first conference in 2009 covered both the art and the science of automotive audio: audio evaluation, wideband speech communication, initiating natural spoken dialogue, signal processing for multichannel sound, acoustic modeling of the small space of a car cabin, advances in microphones, loudspeakers and amplifiers, mobile internet audio, digital audio networks, active noise control in cars, and audio cues designed for hybrid and electric vehicles. Most of these are still the main topics in automotive audio today. Forty-two years after the first branded sound system was installed in a car, the industry is making enormous progress. Sound-system integration now runs through the architecture of the car itself. The auto industry is changing faster than ever: electrification is changing how people think about vehicles, software development and deployment matter more than ever before, and young car brands are disrupting the industry.

Speaking of disruption, I can’t leave out this week’s headline story in the German media: the job cuts at Volkswagen. Hit hard by Chinese new-energy vehicles, Volkswagen, which sells half its cars in China, has posted dismal results and is having to smash with its own hands the “iron rice bowl” of job security it once gave its workers. Three of its plants in Germany are to close, nearly 10,000 jobs are to go, and the pay and benefits of the staff who remain are being cut. Beyond being out-competed at home in China and losing the price war, innovation is what these traditional carmakers most need to commit to.

Working across disciplines

Advanced audio processing was a hot topic at the conference, extending even to neural networks and machine learning for source separation and speech enhancement, and to equalizing and optimizing loudspeakers when creating immersive audio in the car. There was also work on optimizing cabin acoustics, from active noise control to individual sound zones for each passenger: personalized experiences are increasingly the focus. This field is sure to develop further, and I expect deeper discussion and new progress at the next AES Automotive Audio Conference.

But how do you bring together the huge amount of R&D now going on in individual OEM programs? One particularly interesting session at the conference looked at how to upgrade the audio ecosystem to deliver a future-proof audio architecture that meets the needs of a personalized car environment. The discussion also touched on the Audio Foundry, launched in 2023. Initiated by Tymphany, this collaborative workspace now has labs in Wales in the UK and in Silicon Valley, California, and aims to give companies and integrators in the automotive industry a platform for joint innovation that improves the audio ecosystem as a whole.

The discussion “Synergizing NVH, Sound, and Speech: Innovating Automotive Design” pointed out an interesting phenomenon: at the big OEMs, the walls between the NVH department and the automotive audio departments (speech recognition, audio design and so on) are high. Breaking down those walls and working together more closely would bring big advantages in building adaptable, future-proof systems. It would not only improve the user experience across all driving conditions, but also cut costs and raise efficiency.

New directions in audio

Innovation in signal processing and speech, and its convergence with AI, is driving applications on many fronts.

Another core topic was Active Sound Design. The concept was fiercely controversial in the days of combustion-engine cars, but it has now become an important part of electric vehicles (EVs). As the audio architectures of new vehicle programs offer immersive audio and variable acoustics, and open up unprecedented possibilities for designers of EV sound systems, there will be many new ways to explore active sound design.

The article mentions an integrated approach that can “transform brand values into sound, implementing software for DSPs and control units, as well as hardware integration and fine-tuning of physical prototypes.” Having read it, I felt it said a great deal and, at the same time, nothing at all. I didn’t fully understand it, so I’ll leave readers to interpret it for themselves. “Brand audio” is another concept that comes up a lot these days (for now I’m rendering it in Chinese as “sound brand”). The goal is for people to recognize a car by its sound alone, without seeing the logo. That is good news for people in acoustics and audio: it shows that attention is no longer only on what we see and is starting to shift toward what we hear.

Besides sound designs that start from the sound of a traditional combustion engine and combine it with additive or granular synthesis, some have proposed letting users choose their own sounds. There is also haptic feedback synchronized with the seats. But challenges remain, for example: “the vehicles’ networks are changing (with important implications in control logic and sound triggers), and the automotive audio platforms currently adjusting to software-defined vehicles.”

I looked up haptic feedback on Meridian’s website. Roughly, the idea is that besides the sound your ears hear, you also need vibration your body can feel. At a concert, for example, it only feels real if, along with the sound, you feel the bass rumbling through your seat. Here, that haptic feedback is delivered as vibration through the car seat. Loudspeakers and sensors

The demo cars routinely had twenty or thirty loudspeakers, and many also offered Dolby audio and upmixed music (I’m still not sure what the standard Chinese term for “upmix” is), giving a strong sense of space (spatial, immersive, 3D).

In-car loudspeakers come in all shapes and forms. Hyundai’s MOBIS Live Dynamic sound system places exciters in the headrests, using Flexound’s technology. The account shared one of their videos a while ago:

Tesla does without loudspeakers and instead makes the various surfaces of the car’s interior trim vibrate to produce sound (I’m not sure how good it sounds).

These demos also showed that signal-processing tools can do a great deal acoustically with the loudspeakers a car already has, and that there is still plenty of room to explore.

Sennheiser can split stereo music into its different components in real time and then use the existing loudspeaker system to send each component to a different position, recreating the original artistic intent as faithfully as possible. There is also an “Immersion slider” that controls how immersive the sound is. It can cater not only to the driver’s seat but also to other passengers, such as the boss in the VIP seat at the right rear.

From DSP to ecosystem

In the era of the software-defined vehicle, audio is becoming a new arena for innovation and differentiation. OEMs now need advanced audio software platforms to develop, deploy and upgrade audio features over the entire life of the vehicle, and to work out what this means for new business models and opportunities.

Paul Beckmann of DSP Concepts issued a challenge to the industry: he proposed building a “third-party IP ecosystem” around audio processing units (APUs) and standardized, application-oriented APIs, with the aim of creating dedicated chips for audio acceleration.

He pointed out that even the graphics systems in today’s cars benefit from industry collaboration in the 1990s, such as OpenGL, released by Silicon Graphics in 1992, and DirectX, launched by Microsoft in 1995. These drove the standardization of APIs and cross-platform support, which ultimately made hardware acceleration possible and gave rise to the graphics processing unit (GPU). GPUs are chips designed specifically to accelerate graphics; they are complex and hard to program, but application developers never have to see those details.

Audio systems in 2024, by contrast, depend on solutions from many different vendors (Qualcomm, Samsung, ADI, Texas Instruments and others), each with its own proprietary API. That makes product development difficult, and the problem only grows as applications become more complex.

With its Audio Weaver framework, DSP Concepts is already working to simplify this process by offering standardized APIs and cross-platform support. But Paul Beckmann proposed a broader initiative: a joint effort to advance the new concept of the audio processing unit (APU), so that, through standardized application-oriented APIs, the audio field can make use of dedicated audio-acceleration chips while also benefiting from advances in machine learning.

The goal may seem distant, but given the transformation audio systems are going through and the exponentially growing demand for hardware acceleration, the initiative has a real chance. As he put it, “it may not be too late to start now.”

Interested readers can turn to the conference paper by Paul Beckmann, John Whitecar and Steve Ernst, “Leveraging Multiple Threads and Cores for Advanced Automotive Audio Processing,” which discusses in detail the key techniques and methods for optimizing audio processing in automotive systems.

(A quick search shows that NVIDIA already has an APU for PCs: https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/drivers/apu/)

Source: audioXpress, October 2024 / 5th International AES Conference on Automotive Audio
